note: Fourteen new records for the supply-chain-and-release-integrity capability, read 2026-08-15. Five ledgered records already cover adjacent ground and are cited rather than re-recorded: EV-0038 (SLSA v1.2 verifying artifacts), EV-0068 (Sigstore overview), EV-0069 (OpenSSF Scorecard), EV-0155 (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH) and EV-0156 (Bazel hermeticity). One source refused automated access and is recorded as a gap in NOTES.md rather than as a record: the CISA 2025 minimum elements for an SBOM returned HTTP 403.

records.licence: Community Specification License 1.0 (stated on the specification pages, Linux Foundation)
records.finding: The threat model is organised by where in the chain the attacker acts: at the source, during the build, at publication, in the distribution channel, and at the point the consumer picks a package. Each entry names the level that mitigates it, and several entries say plainly that no level does. A producer who deliberately ships bad code, compromise of the source-control platform itself, typosquatting at selection time, insecure use of a correct artefact, and build-time dependency compromise are all outside what the build track claims, with dependencies handled only by suggesting the framework be applied recursively to each one.
records.applicability_limits: A framework rather than a measurement: it names threat classes and level requirements, gives no acceptance thresholds, and its levels describe the build platform's properties rather than the artefact's safety. The source track was only promoted out of experimental in v1.2, so its requirements have had little adversarial use.

records.source: in-toto Attestation Framework, Statement layer specification
records.version_or_commit: spec/v1, repository main branch at 898 commits
records.finding: An attestation is layered so the claim and the thing claimed about are separable: a signed envelope wraps a statement, the statement binds a list of subjects to a predicate type, and the predicate carries whatever the claim actually is. Every subject must carry a digest, and subjects are matched by digest alone regardless of what the file is called or what type it is. That is the property worth copying: a claim travels with the hash it is about, so renaming or repackaging an artefact silently detaches the claim rather than silently transferring it.
records.applicability_limits: The framework fixes a shape, not a meaning. Whether a given predicate is worth trusting depends entirely on who signed it and how the predicate type is defined elsewhere, and the specification says nothing about either. The project describes its tooling integration as still under development.

records.source: PEP 740, Index support for digital attestations
records.version_or_commit: Final, created 2024-01-08, accepted 2024-07-17; now marked historical with the live specification moved to the PyPA specifications page
records.licence: Public domain and CC0-1.0-Universal dual dedication, which PEP 1 requires of every PEP
records.finding: The index-attestation design binds a distribution filename and its SHA-256 digest inside an in-toto v1 statement, carries the signature alongside verification material including the signing certificate and its transparency-log entry, and identifies the publisher by a trusted-publisher kind plus a claims object holding the authentication context. The design note that matters is the scope limit the authors wrote into it: attestations do not raise or lower trust in the index, because an index that is itself dishonest can still alter what it serves or simply omit the attestation.
records.applicability_limits: Deliberately silent on policy. It does not say attestations must exist, does not say an installer must check them, and leaves both to index operators and package managers, so the presence of the mechanism tells you nothing about whether anybody in a given ecosystem is verifying.
records.counter_evidence: Its own omission-attack note is the counter-evidence to any claim that a present, valid attestation proves the artefact is what the project released: absence is unsigned and therefore unverifiable, so a verifier that accepts unattested artefacts gains nothing from the ones that are attested.

records.source: CycloneDX specification overview, OWASP and Ecma TC54
records.licence: Apache-2.0 on the specification repository (stated in the repository); the overview page itself states no licence for the page content
records.finding: The bill of materials is not only a component list. The same document model carries services the software calls out to, the dependency relationships between components, known vulnerabilities, the formulation that describes how the thing was actually built, declarations of conformance with attached evidence, and compositions that record how complete each part of the inventory is claimed to be. The completeness field is the underrated one: a bill of materials that cannot say which of its branches are partial invites the reader to treat a gap as an absence.
records.applicability_limits: A format, not a method of discovery. Nothing in the specification makes a generator find what is actually there, and the richer sections (formulation, declarations) are optional, so two conforming documents about one artefact can differ enormously in what they claim.

records.licence: Community Specification License (stated in the specification repository LICENSE.md)
records.finding: Repository integrity is split across four roles so that no single key compromise is fatal: a root role that delegates trust and is kept offline, a targets role that says which files are trusted, a snapshot role that pins the set of metadata versions that go together, and a timestamp role that is online and therefore deliberately given the least to lose. Each role needs a threshold of signatures rather than one. The attacks this shape defends against are the ones a plain signature does not touch: serving an older signed release, replaying stale metadata so a client never learns an update exists, and mixing metadata from different points in time.
records.applicability_limits: Aimed at whoever runs a repository, not at a single project publishing into someone else's. A venture consuming from a registry inherits whatever the registry implements and cannot add roles to it; the useful reading for a small venture is which attacks its registry leaves open rather than a plan to deploy the framework.

records.licence: MIT stated on the sigstore/docs repository; the page itself carries no separate content licence
records.finding: The certificate authority issues code-signing certificates that live for ten minutes and bind an OpenID Connect identity rather than a key the signer keeps. The private key is generated for one signing operation and can be discarded, which removes key custody as an ongoing problem and replaces it with dependence on an identity provider and on a public log that records what was issued. It runs as a public shared instance, and can also be self-hosted where an organisation wants to own the trust root.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor documentation for the project's own design, not an evaluation. Ten minutes is stated as the certificate lifetime at this access and is an operational parameter of the public instance rather than a specification constant. Verification after the certificate has expired depends on the log entry, so the availability and honesty of the log is load-bearing in a way a long-lived key is not.
records.counter_evidence: Trading key custody for identity-provider dependence moves the compromise target rather than removing it: whoever can obtain a token for the publishing identity can obtain a valid certificate, and the ten-minute window bounds only how long that one certificate is directly usable.

records.version_or_commit: documentation site as at 2026-08-15; feature requires npm 9.5.0 or later
records.licence: CC BY 4.0 for documentation content, MIT for code, per the npm/documentation repository
records.finding: Registry provenance publishes a verifiable link from a package to the source repository and build instructions that produced it, generated from a hosted build platform's identity token, currently GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD. It requires the package metadata to name a public repository matching where the publish ran. The documentation states its own limit in one line: a package with established provenance is not thereby free of malicious code. Consumers check with a single command over an installed tree rather than per artefact at fetch time.
records.applicability_limits: Ecosystem-specific and platform-specific. It cannot describe a build that ran anywhere other than a supported hosted platform, and a private repository cannot use it at all, so a venture that builds locally or on its own runners gets nothing from this mechanism regardless of how careful its process is.

records.source: npm CLI configuration reference, min-release-age and min-release-age-exclude
records.version_or_commit: npm CLI v11 documentation as at 2026-08-15; min-release-age added in 11.10.0, per-package exclusion in 11.19.0
records.licence: CC BY 4.0 for documentation content, MIT for code, per the npm/documentation repository
records.finding: The client can refuse to resolve any version published more recently than a configured number of days, defaulting to off, with a glob list of package names exempted from the window. The interaction with vulnerability remediation is stated rather than hidden: when the window blocks the patched version, the install keeps the vulnerable one, warns, and exits non-zero. So the control is a deliberate trade of patch latency for exposure to freshly published malicious versions, and the tool makes you see the trade rather than making it for you.
records.applicability_limits: One ecosystem's client. The window is measured from publish time as the registry reports it, so it assumes the registry's timestamps are honest and that a malicious version is not simply held back until the window has passed.

records.licence: AGPL-3.0 (renovatebot/renovate repository licence file, read directly)
records.finding: The same delay implemented in an update bot rather than the install client, with three caveats the maintainers state outright. Updates classified as security fixes bypass the delay entirely. The clock is per version, not per package, so a fast-releasing project is not held back indefinitely. And on registries where a tag can be re-pushed, notably container registries, re-pushing an existing tag restarts the clock, which means the delay can be sidestepped by the same actor it is meant to slow down.
records.applicability_limits: Bot-side rather than install-side, so it governs what gets proposed, not what a developer or an agent can install by hand. The security-update bypass is a policy choice made by the tool's own classification of what counts as a security update.
records.counter_evidence: The re-push caveat is counter-evidence against applying one cooldown policy uniformly across ecosystems: it works where versions are immutable and degrades to nothing where tags are mutable.

records.source: Go modules reference, checksum database and vendoring
records.licence: not stated on the page; go.dev content is published by the Go project under the terms linked from its site footer
records.finding: Two integrity mechanisms sit side by side and behave differently. The lock file records a hash per module version and the public checksum database is the transparency log that makes those hashes hard to rewrite after the fact, which buys authenticity, meaning the bytes are the bytes that were released, and buys nothing about whether those bytes are safe. Vendoring changes the picture: with a vendor directory in use, builds load packages from the tree and the tool checks only that the vendored manifest agrees with the module file. Hash verification is not repeated at build time, so vendoring moves the verification to the moment the directory was generated and to whoever reviews the diff afterwards.
records.applicability_limits: One language's toolchain, and one with unusually strong defaults; ecosystems whose lock files are advisory, or whose installers run arbitrary code at install time, do not inherit any of this. The vendoring behaviour described is the default from the toolchain version that made vendor directories automatic onwards.

records.source: GitHub Actions documentation, security hardening for workflows
records.licence: CC BY 4.0 for documentation content, MIT for code, per the github/docs repository
records.finding: The blast radius of a build system is written down here in plain terms. Anyone with write access to the repository can read every configured secret. Untrusted text arriving from a pull request reaches shell context and is an injection route unless it is passed through an intermediate variable or a dedicated action. A third-party step referenced by tag is mutable and only a full commit digest is immutable. Self-hosted runners offer no isolation guarantee and can be persistently compromised, which is why they should not serve public repositories. The default token should be read-only and widened per job.
records.applicability_limits: One platform's guidance, describing its own controls, and it is guidance rather than an enforced default: nothing here fails a build if it is ignored. The pull-request injection route depends on which trigger a workflow uses, which the page treats at a level of detail a reader still has to apply themselves.

records.source: Schorlemmer et al., Signing in Four Public Software Package Registries: Quantity, Quality, and Influencing Factors
records.study_design: longitudinal measurement of signature presence and signature validity across four registries, with an analysis of what preceded changes in adoption
records.population: artefacts published to Maven Central, PyPI, Docker Hub and Hugging Face over 2023
records.version_or_commit: arXiv v2, 2024-04-14; published at IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2024
records.licence: arXiv non-exclusive licence to distribute (arXiv nonexclusive-distrib 1.0), as shown on the abstract page
records.finding: Signing is rare where it is not compulsory and unreliable where it is. In the measured year, roughly 97 percent of Maven Central artefacts carried a signature against about 1 percent on Docker Hub, 0.2 percent on PyPI and 0.1 percent on Hugging Face. Validity was worse than presence: about 27 percent of Maven Central signatures, 52 percent of PyPI signatures and 76 percent of Hugging Face signatures failed verification, with over 99 percent of the Maven and PyPI failures traced to public keys that were expired, revoked or simply not findable. Mandates moved quantity, dedicated tooling moved quality, and known attacks moved neither.
records.applicability_limits: One year, four registries, and a definition of failure the authors flag as their own judgement: an expired or revoked key counts as a failure regardless of whether it was valid when the signature was made. Key discovery relied on published locations, so keys distributed privately or on small sites read as missing. Third-party metadata sources may carry errors.
records.counter_evidence: This is the counter-evidence to treating a signature as a control. Presence of a signature is not evidence of anything unless somebody verifies it, and on three of the four registries measured, the majority or near-majority of what was there would not verify.

records.source: Zhou, Dacier and Konstantinou, A Reality Check on SBOM-based Vulnerability Management
records.study_design: large-scale generation and scanning study, with a manual case study establishing ground truth for the false-positive measurement
records.licence: CC BY 4.0, as shown on the abstract page
records.finding: The bill of materials is only as good as how it was made, and the alert stream coming off it is mostly noise. Generating from lock files with a strong package manager produced accurate and consistent inventories where other routes did not. Against that inventory, the vulnerability scanners in the case study reported false positives at about 92 percent, and adding reachability analysis over the call graph removed roughly 62 percent of those alarms. The cause the authors identify is vulnerable code that is present but never called.
records.applicability_limits: The 92 percent figure comes from a case study rather than from the full 2,414-repository set, so it is an illustration of scale rather than a population estimate. Open-source repositories only, and reachability analysis is itself language-dependent and approximate.
records.counter_evidence: It cuts against demanding a generated bill of materials for its own sake: the same paper shows the inventory is trustworthy mainly when it is derived from a lock file that already exists, which is an argument for pinning first and generating second.

records.source: Santos-Grueiro, On Good Authority: Release-Authority Measurement for Registry-Mediated Package Ecosystems
records.study_design: observational measurement of change in the publishing path between consecutive releases, with practitioner review of a sample of the flagged cases
records.population: 45,812 releases across npm, PyPI, Maven Central, crates.io and RubyGems
records.licence: CC BY 4.0, as shown on the abstract page
records.finding: Watching how a release was published, rather than what it contains, is a cheap and independent signal. Comparing publisher, repository, workflow, provenance and signing evidence between consecutive releases surfaced 204 discontinuities worth review across the measured set, and a single distance rule flagged 320 releases covering 190 of them. Practitioners reviewing 30 of the core cases judged 20 to warrant immediate attention and 9 continued monitoring, which is a usable precision for a signal that costs nothing to compute at admission time.
records.applicability_limits: The authors state the boundary themselves: a compromise that reuses the same public publishing path, a build system that is already compromised and unchanged, and versions missing from public snapshots all leave no discontinuity to find. Practitioner review covered 30 cases, so the precision estimate is small-sample.
records.counter_evidence: A high-cadence project that legitimately migrates its release workflow generates the same signal as a compromise, so the rule is a prompt to look rather than a verdict, and a consumer who treats every discontinuity as an incident will spend most of that attention on ordinary maintenance.
